prime.problem: Divide without *, / or %: subtracting the divisor until you can't is correct but needs 2,147,483,648 steps for −2³¹ / −1, and that same input overflows a 32-bit int. You need division in about log² n steps and a careful sign and range story.
prime.fits: First maths card. It opens the "fewer steps" family from the overview: instead of caching states, skip ahead by powers of two. The same doubling idea returns in square-and-multiply on the modular-arithmetic card.
prime.goal: Divide by doubling the divisor, explain why the quotient's bits are the chunks taken, and handle truncation, sign and the −2³¹ / −1 overflow.

attend: Why is each chunk subtracted a divisor-sized power of two, and how does that make the quotient's binary digits?
Why does the inner loop stop one doubling before it would overshoot?
Why is −2³¹ / −1 the only quotient that can overflow 32 bits?
Why take absolute values first, and why is that itself dangerous in a 32-bit language?
How does x & −x isolate the lowest set bit?

must: Write a = Σ b·2<sup>k</sup> + r → each round finds the biggest b·2<sup>k</sup> ≤ what's left by doubling → subtract it and set bit k of q → q's set bits are exactly the chunks → O(log² n) shift-compares instead of O(a/b) subtractions (174 vs 142,857,142 for 10⁹ / 7)

Two's complement stores −x as 2<sup>w</sup> − x → the range is [−2³¹, 2³¹ − 1], one more negative than positive → −2³¹ has no positive twin → −2³¹ / −1 = 2³¹ overflows, and the problem clamps it to 2³¹ − 1
// and >> floor toward −∞ but the problem truncates toward 0 → −7 / 2 must be −3, not −4 → divide absolute values and fix the sign once at the end
elevated: In a 32-bit language abs(−2³¹) overflows back to −2³¹ → widen to 64 bits or run the loop on negatives (the larger side of the range)
Each round restarts doubling from b → O(log² n); remembering the chunk list and walking it back down once makes it O(log n)

compress.prompt: From memory, trace 43 / 8 as rounds of doubling, write 43 as a sum of divisor-sized powers of two plus a remainder, and state the one input that needs the clamp and why.

retrieve.q: Explain why the quotient's binary representation falls out of the chunks the loop subtracts.
answer: each chunk is b·2<sup>k</sup> for some k
the chunks sum to b·q, so q = Σ 2<sup>k</sup>
each chunk contributes one set bit of q; no k is used twice because each round takes the biggest one that fits

retrieve.q: Walk through 100 / 7: the doublings tried in each round, the chunk taken, and the running quotient.
answer: round 1: 14, 28, 56 fit, 112 doesn't → take 56, q = 8, left 44
round 2: 14, 28 fit, 56 doesn't → take 28, q = 12, left 16
round 3: 14 fits, 28 doesn't → take 14, q = 14, left 2; stop

retrieve.q: Repeated subtraction, int(a / b), a // b and shift-and-subtract: which are allowed, which are correct for all 32-bit inputs, and what does each cost?
answer: repeated subtraction: allowed, correct, but O(a/b): 2³¹ steps worst case
int(a / b): banned, goes through a float (wrong past 2⁵³)
a // b: banned and floors instead of truncating
shift-and-subtract: allowed, at most 496 steps, exact

compare.q: Shift-and-subtract division and square-and-multiply both build an answer one power of two at a time. What is doubled in each, and what decides whether a bit is used?
answer: division doubles the divisor; a bit of q is set when that chunk still fits
fast power squares the base; a bit of the exponent decides whether to multiply it in
both take O(log) steps where the naive method takes O(n)

compare.q: The Fenwick tree moves by i += i & −i. What does two's complement guarantee about i & −i, and why is that the right step size?
answer: −i = ~i + 1 flips every bit above the lowest 1 and keeps that 1
so i & −i is exactly the lowest set bit
each Fenwick cell covers a block whose size is its lowest set bit, so this jumps to the next responsible cell

predict.q: Predict how many rounds and shift-compares divide(2**30, 1) takes, compared with divide(2**31 − 1, 1)'s 496.
predict.answer: One round and 31 shift-compares: the doubling climbs 1, 2, 4, … to 2³⁰ (30 that fit, one that overshoots), subtracts everything and stops. The number of rounds equals the number of set bits in the quotient: 2³⁰ has one, 2³¹ − 1 has 31.

apply.task: Trace divide(100, 7) by hand, counting shift-compares as the card does (every doubling test, including the one that fails). Then compute 40 & −40 and 40 & 39 on paper in 8-bit binary.
apply.hint: 39 = 00100111: subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 and every 0 below it.

reflect: Could you explain two's complement's lopsided range without drawing bits?
Which prediction did you get wrong: rounds = set bits of q, or the 2³⁰ count?
Which link is fuzzy: chunks → quotient bits, or truncation → abs first, sign last?
Where have you used x & −x or x & (x − 1) before?
What will you look for in Newton's method, which also gains more than one step at a time?
